sections.overview: The meadow grasshopper is a widespread European grass-feeding acridid found in meadows and other open grassy habitats. Many modern European lists use Pseudochorthippus parallelus, while Chorthippus parallelus remains common in regional literature and data systems.
sections.identification: Adults are usually green or brown, and colour varies within the species. The side keels on the pronotum are approximately parallel, a useful clue against similar grasshoppers such as the common green grasshopper C. viridulus, though careful identification may require song or close examination.
sections.habitat: It occurs across a wide range of grasslands, field margins and woodland edges, with particularly frequent records in moist or moderately productive swards. It is common in much of Germany and France, but local abundance depends on vegetation structure and management.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on grasses, cropping blades with its chewing mouthparts.
sections.behavior: Males produce a soft stridulating song to attract females, and adults are most often seen in the warmer months. It is a short-winged, mainly ground-dwelling grasshopper, though some individuals have longer wings and can disperse farther.
sections.reproduction: After mating, females deposit egg pods in soil; the eggs overwinter and nymphs hatch in spring. The species has one main generation each year in much of its temperate range, with development timing shifting with local climate.
sections.ecology: It is food for birds and other insect-eaters and can be a dominant herbivore in grassland. Its close relative C. montanus is associated more strongly with wet, marshy grassland, so habitat overlap does not make the two interchangeable.
sections.conservation: A German species summary considers it widespread and not threatened in Germany; that local assessment should not be extrapolated to every region.
